title: Confession rites
hook: from the Orthodox confession before an icon to the general confession in a prayer book

segments.voice: Yesterday, unction: a little case of oil, a hospital corridor, and the elders coming when they're called. Your line was oil and prayer. What ordinary thing did you do for someone unwell? Day one thousand three hundred forty-nine.

In a small Orthodox church, a woman stands at a lectern near the front, facing an icon of Christ, with a Gospel book and a cross resting there. The priest stands beside her, not across from her. They're both looking at the icon. She speaks quietly. When she's finished, she bows her head, and he lays the end of his stole over it and prays. Across town, in a church with a prayer book in every pew, a whole congregation kneels, and nobody says anything private at all. Instead, every voice in the room says the same words at once: "We have left undone those things which we ought to have done." Today: confession rites.

Christians confess in different rooms, but the rooms lean on the same two lines. The first comes one verse after yesterday's oil. James writes, in the King James Bible: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." Confession, in James, is spoken out loud to another person. The second is from the first letter of John: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." Now, three rooms. First, the Orthodox. The person confessing stands before an icon of Christ, with the priest beside them. In some Orthodox prayers before confession, the priest describes himself as only a witness: it's Christ who hears and forgives. Second, the Catholic sacrament of penance, often called reconciliation. A person tells their sins to a priest in private, behind a screen or face to face, and hears the words of absolution. The priest is bound by the seal of confession: he may never repeat what he heard. Third, the general confession. In the old English prayer book, the whole congregation says it together: "We have left undone those things which we ought to have done; And we have done those things which we ought not to have done." Some Protestant services include a prayer of confession like it, followed by words of forgiveness. Notice the order inside that pair of lines. Left undone comes before done. Ahead of the wrong things done, it names the good things nobody got around to: the visit, the apology, the help. Whether whispered to a priest, said before an icon, or spoken by a whole kneeling room, the shape is the same. Say it out loud. Hear that it's forgiven.

Here's the practice: confess one thing. Settle, and breathe. Don't make a list. Look for just one thing. It might be something you did. Or, following the prayer book, something you left undone: the call you didn't make, the thank-you you never said, the help you saw was needed and walked past. Name it plainly to yourself, without excuses and without piling on. If you pray, you can bring it to God and rest on the promise in John's letter: faithful and just to forgive. If you don't, simply let it be named, and notice what changes when it is. The bell holds the time.
Confession rites. The church's ways of saying sin out loud and hearing it forgiven: before an icon, to a priest in private, or all together from a prayer book.
Your line: we have left undone. Today, do one thing you've been leaving undone: the email, the apology, the visit. Just one. Day one thousand three hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians confess before an icon of Christ with a priest beside them; Catholics confess privately to a priest in the sacrament of penance and receive absolution; Anglican, Lutheran and some other Protestant services include a general confession said together, followed by a declaration of forgiveness.

fork.setup: you've wronged a friend in your church, and you're reading the letter of James. what does it tell you to do?
options: say nothing and hope it fades.
confess your faults one to another, and pray for one another.
wait for your friend to bring it up first.
fork.reveal: "confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." in James, confession is spoken, and it heals.

original.note: Greek: confess, the verb in James 5:16, telling believers to confess to one another.

trapdoor: what you thought: confession means a dark booth and a list of sins.
what it means: the church's rites for saying sin out loud and hearing it forgiven, privately or all together.
what a scholar hears: in the general confession's paired lines, what was left undone is named before what was done.

notes: Hook: Orthodox scene (icon, Gospel book and cross on a stand, priest beside the penitent, epitrachelion laid over the head with the prayer of absolution) given as one scene; practice varies by jurisdiction. Confirm.
'In some Orthodox prayers before confession, the priest describes himself as only a witness' paraphrases the exhortation used in Slavonic-tradition churches; confirm.
BCP 1662 General Confession (Morning Prayer) quoted; confirm exact capitalization and punctuation.
'Many Protestant services include a prayer of confession' — confirm or soften to 'some'.
Original: ἐξομολογεῖσθε (present imperative, James 5:16); confirm accent and transliteration.

Audit pass: 'left undone comes first' overstated the text: the 1662 General Confession already confesses wrongs done ('followed too much the devices and desires of our own hearts', 'offended against thy holy laws') before this pair. Teach, screen head, myth and trapdoor now say 'within the pair'. Doubled 'small' in the hook cut.
Editor pass: garbled 'stands at a stand' fixed; James 5:16 is an instruction, so 'two promises' became 'two lines'; 'many Protestant services' softened to 'some'.
